title: Alibaba open-sources AI model that can detect cancer and nearly 150 conditions
content:
Alibaba open-sources medical AI model that can detect cancer and nearly 150 conditions
Tested on nearly 40,000 real-world exams, the model outperformed most radiologists, according to a new study published in Science
Alibaba Group Holding’s research arm, Damo Academy, has open-sourced an artificial intelligence model capable of identifying nearly 150 abdominal conditions – including cancers – by reading computed tomography (CT) scans, marking the latest step in the firm’s growing medical AI efforts.
The vision-language model, called Damo Radar, was designed to analyse contrast-enhanced CT scans covering 18 abdominal organs and identify a broad range of diseases and other abnormalities, such as malignant tumours, the institute said on Friday.
The model was trained using CT scans paired with clinical reports. In nearly 40,000 real-world examinations, it achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.913 across 146 clinical findings. An AUC of 1.0 represents perfect diagnostic accuracy.
The research team said the training method could eventually be extended to other types of medical imaging, calling the model “the world’s first expert-level generalist medical imaging model”.

report.summary: Alibaba's Damo Academy open-sources Damo Radar, a CT-scan AI that detects nearly 150 abdominal conditions, including cancers, and outperformed most radiologists in a study.
report.background: Alibaba's Damo Academy has been expanding into medical AI as large vision-language models mature. The new model, Damo Radar, arrives amid growing demand for tools that can help radiologists handle rising CT scan volumes and detect cancers earlier. Open-sourcing the model lets researchers and hospitals inspect, adapt, and validate it, which is important in regulated healthcare. The study, published in Science, claims it outperformed most radiologists across 146 findings, adding credibility to generalist medical imaging models. It also reflects a broader industry race among Chinese and global tech firms to build foundation models for healthcare, where data, clinical validation, and regulation are key barriers.
key_points: Damo Radar is a vision-language AI model that reads contrast-enhanced CT scans covering 18 abdominal organs. It can flag nearly 150 conditions, including malignant tumours and other abnormalities, according to Alibaba's Damo Academy. The system is designed as a generalist imaging expert rather than a narrow, single-disease detector.

It was trained by pairing CT scans with clinical reports. In nearly 40,000 real-world exams, it reached an average AUC of 0.913 across 146 clinical findings. AUC measures diagnostic accuracy, with 1.0 being perfect. That result suggests strong performance across many conditions, not just one.

The research team says Damo Radar outperformed most radiologists in the study published in Science. They call it the world's first expert-level generalist medical imaging model. The same training method could be extended to other imaging types, such as X-rays or MRIs, potentially broadening its clinical use.

Alibaba has open-sourced the model, making it available for researchers, developers, and hospitals to test and build on. It is the latest step in Damo Academy's medical AI push. Open-sourcing may speed innovation, but clinical deployment will still require regulatory approval, local validation, and integration into hospital workflows.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Damo Radar signals that generalist medical imaging models are moving from research demos toward clinically benchmarked tools. Open-sourcing lowers barriers for developers, who can fine-tune or audit the model instead of training from scratch, and intensifies competition in medical foundation models. For developers, it creates opportunities in data pipelines, evaluation, regulatory tooling, and hospital integration. For regular users, the promise is faster, more consistent CT reads and earlier detection, especially where radiologists are scarce. But risks remain: model errors, dataset bias, privacy, and overreliance without human oversight. Real-world benefit depends on rigorous validation and transparent deployment.
report.tools: Watch Alibaba DAMO Academy's GitHub and ModelScope releases for Damo Radar weights and code. Related open-source projects for medical imaging include MONAI, nnU-Net, and TotalSegmentator for segmentation and pipelines; LLaVA-Med and RadFM for medical vision-language research; and MedMNIST for lightweight benchmarking. Hospitals and developers should also track DICOM tooling and evaluation frameworks to test performance on local data before clinical use.
